manifest.name: dsh-hebrew-rtl
manifest.description: Correct Hebrew RTL rendering for the DeepSeek Harness web GUI: any line with Hebrew reads right-to-left, bidi-safe input fields, and RTL-aware Cmd+Left/Right line navigation.

scripts.test: node scripts/smoke-test.mjs && node scripts/browser-test.mjs && node scripts/fields-browser-test.mjs

bundle.text:
# dsh-hebrew-rtl bundle patch.
#
# Declared through `dsh.bundle.patch` in package.json, which is what makes the
# package installable with `dsh plugin add`. The row it inserts mounts the
# package's host half; the client half is discovered separately from the
# `dsh.client` declaration and served to the browser by the client module
# registry, so it needs no row of its own.
- insert:
    - id: hebrew-rtl
      name: dsh-hebrew-rtl

readme.section: dsh-hebrew-rtl
readme.text:
English | [עברית](./README.he.md)

Correct Hebrew RTL rendering for the [DeepSeek Harness](https://github.com/deepseek-harness/harness) web GUI: any line with Hebrew reads right-to-left, bidi-safe input fields, and RTL-aware `Cmd`+`←`/`→` line navigation.

readme.section: The problem
readme.text: The GUI renders every block left-to-right. For Hebrew that produces three distinct failures:

readme.section: The problem
readme.text:
1. **Whole paragraphs read backwards.** A Hebrew sentence is laid out as an LTR paragraph, so its lines start on the wrong side and punctuation lands at the wrong end.
2. **Typing into a field runs the wrong way.** The `ask_user_question` custom-answer field inherits the page direction, so Hebrew typed into it flows left-to-right.
3. **`Cmd`+`←`/`→` feel inverted.** These shortcuts are *logical* in every browser: `←` goes to the line's logical start, which on an RTL line sits at the visual **right** edge. Pressing `←` jumps the caret to the far right.

readme.section: The problem
readme.text: The obvious CSS answer — `unicode-bidi: plaintext` — fixes only the easy half. It picks a block's direction from its **first strong directional character**, so a Hebrew sentence that opens with a Latin product name, a list number, or an emoji is still rendered LTR and still reads garbled.

readme.section: Any line with Hebrew in it is RTL
readme.text:
The rule is deliberately blunt: a block (`p`, `ul`/`ol`, `h1`–`h6`, `blockquote`, `table`) or a line of text that contains **even one Hebrew letter** is forced to `direction: rtl` + `text-align: right`. A block with no Hebrew is left to `unicode-bidi: plaintext`.

Forced blocks get `unicode-bidi: isolate`, so the Unicode Bidi algorithm still lays out the Latin runs correctly **inside** the RTL line:

readme.section: Any line with Hebrew in it is RTL
readme.text:
```
Rollout: מוסיפים minPodsPerReplicaSet: 2
→ RTL: "Rollout:" reads first, on the right; the identifiers stay unreversed

DSH הוא כלי מצוין לעבודה יומיומית.

readme.section: Any line with Hebrew in it is RTL
readme.text: **Why not count which script dominates.** Earlier versions counted Hebrew words against Latin words and followed the majority. Mixed technical Hebrew is the normal case, not the edge case: `Rollout: מוסיפים minPodsPerReplicaSet: 2`, `canonical-revision=canary. minAvailable: 50% ... בוחר רק pods עם` — each has more Latin than Hebrew and came out LTR, line after line, in otherwise Hebrew answers. The accepted cost: an English sentence carrying a single Hebrew word is RTL too.

readme.section: Any line with Hebrew in it is RTL
readme.text:
**Lines outside paragraphs.** GenUI components (steps, lists, tables, callouts…), `ask_user_question` cards and your own message bubble render text in ``/`
` elements, not `

`. With `unicode-bidi: plaintext` each of those picked its own direction from its first strong character, so a step titled `1. Rollout: מוסיפים ...` was LTR even inside an RTL list. The plugin now walks the text in the conversation, question cards and GenUI blocks, and forces RTL on the element that lays out each Hebrew line (and on any inline span between the text and that element). The sidebars and settings are not touched.

readme.section: Any line with Hebrew in it is RTL
readme.text: **Components are laid out as a whole.** Which side a question card's option numbers, a GenUI step's markers, or a table's columns sit on is a property of the whole component, so it follows the component's dominant script: a Hebrew question card or GenUI block is laid out RTL (markers and numbers on the right), while an English GenUI table with one Hebrew value keeps its English layout — the Hebrew value itself still reads RTL.

readme.section: Any line with Hebrew in it is RTL
readme.text: **Where dominance is still used: the message and the component.** Dominance no longer decides a line, but it still decides two things that are not a line: which direction a whole message takes (so its all-Latin headings follow it), and a component's layout direction (see above). For those, words are counted and code tokens are excluded. Counting raw letters breaks on technical Hebrew prose. A single identifier can outweigh a whole paragraph — `git+https://git@github.com:kfirsch/...#<sha>` contributes 44 Latin letters by itself, and a commit sha another 40 — so a Hebrew sentence that merely *cites* a URL was rendered LTR. Identifiers, URLs, paths, shas and `15/15`-style ratios are therefore stripped before counting; they are still laid out normally, they just no longer vote on the paragraph's direction. Counting whole words rather than letters follows from the same reasoning: a three-letter Hebrew word says as much about the sentence's language as `credential` does. The stripping is deliberately conservative — an ordinary Latin word standing alone is never treated as code, so genuine English prose still counts in full.

readme.section: Any line with Hebrew in it is RTL
readme.text: **Headings follow their message.** A block on its own is not always enough context. In a Hebrew answer a heading is one line — often a bare identifier such as `agent-sandbox (SIG Apps, kubernetes-sigs)` with no Hebrew in it at all — so judging it alone left it LTR beside its own RTL body, and a document came out alternating sides heading by heading.

readme.section: Any line with Hebrew in it is RTL
readme.text: So each message resolves one direction — Hebrew when more of its paragraphs, lists, tables and quotes carry Hebrew than do not — and a heading with no Hebrew follows it. Two things keep their own direction:

readme.section: Any line with Hebrew in it is RTL
readme.text:
- **A whole paragraph with no Hebrew at all** stays LTR. It is prose in its own right, and forcing RTL on it pushes the run to the far margin and migrates its trailing punctuation to the wrong end. A block inside a Hebrew list or table follows that list or table instead.
- **Code** (`pre`, `code`, and KaTeX) is excluded outright — a code block stays LTR even when it contains Hebrew.

**Composite elements are judged whole, never by their parts.** This one rule was learned three times over:

readme.section: Any line with Hebrew in it is RTL
readme.text:
- **Tables.** Judging each `td` separately gave a six-row status table three different verdicts — Hebrew label cells went RTL while the `HEAD` and `Commits` cells beside them stayed LTR — so the label column changed edges from row to row. Column *order* is a property of the table rather than the cell, so per-cell directions also fight the column order itself.
- **Lists.** The same failure one level down. In a Hebrew numbered list, a short all-Latin item such as `push` has no Hebrew to weigh, so it got no verdict at all, fell back to the page's LTR, and jumped to the opposite margin from its RTL siblings — breaking the numbering column.
- **Formulas.** KaTeX renders a formula as hundreds of nested `<span>`s whose horizontal positions it computes itself. Letting each one pick its own direction tore formulas apart: `(idle + rightsizing)` and `$870/month` came out reordered into nonsense. `.katex` and its whole subtree are excluded — KaTeX handles bidi itself.

readme.section: Any line with Hebrew in it is RTL
readme.text:
So the direction is decided once per composite, from its whole text, and every part inherits it. `unicode-bidi: isolate` still lays out each part's own content correctly within that direction.

Blocks are re-evaluated through a `MutationObserver` as text streams in, coalesced with `requestAnimationFrame` so streaming does not trigger a scan per character.

readme.section: Input fields: any Hebrew, RTL
readme.text:
- **The composer** (a Lexical rich-text editor since dsh `0.1.7`) renders each line as `

`, and `dir="auto"` is first-strong — `Rollout: מוסיפים` came out LTR. Each composer line holding Hebrew is forced RTL. Only the line's inline style is touched, never its content, so the editor's own reconciliation is unaffected. - **Text inputs and textareas** — the session rename dialog, the `ask_user_question` custom answer, search boxes — are forced RTL as a whole when they hold any Hebrew, and released when the Hebrew is gone. The rename dialog opens prefilled and focused, so it is checked on focus as well as on typing. - The custom-answer field is a **two-layer stack**: a hidden height mirror plus the real `

readme.section: RTL-aware line navigation
readme.text: A capture-phase `keydown` listener intercepts `Cmd`+`←`/`→` in text inputs and textareas **only when the caret's current line is RTL** (holds any Hebrew, or sits in a field laid out RTL), and swaps them so each arrow points where the caret visually goes. Lines that are not RTL are left completely untouched. Shift-extension and selection direction are preserved.

readme.section: Install
readme.text:
```sh
dsh plugin --profile web add github:kfirsch/dsh-hebrew-rtl
```

Then restart `dsh web` and hard-refresh the browser tab.

To pin an exact commit (recommended — a later push then cannot silently change what runs):

```sh
dsh plugin --profile web add github:kfirsch/dsh-hebrew-rtl#<commit-sha>
```

The package ships plain hand-written JavaScript in `lib/` with **no build step**, so installing from GitHub needs no `allowBuilds` approval.

readme.section: Uninstall
readme.text:
```sh
dsh plugin --profile web remove dsh-hebrew-rtl
```

readme.section: Scope: Hebrew only, deliberately
readme.text: The direction rule generalises cleanly to every RTL script — Arabic and its languages, Syriac, Thaana, N'Ko, Adlam — and that version was written and passed a 16-case script matrix. It was then **reverted on purpose**: neither the author nor a reviewer can proof-read those scripts, and shipping text-direction handling that nobody involved can verify is worse than not shipping it. The package name says what it actually supports.

readme.section: Scope: Hebrew only, deliberately
readme.text: A pull request adding another script is welcome **from someone who reads it** and can confirm the rendering by eye.

readme.section: Compatibility
readme.text:
- **Surface:** the `web` profile (`dsh web`). No host service, no configuration, no network access.
- **What it never touches:** code blocks — code stays LTR regardless of its content — and contenteditable regions other than the composer.
- Tested against dsh `0.1.7-alpha.1`.

readme.text: [MIT](./LICENSE) © Kfir Schneider

readme.section: For reviewers: why there is no build step
readme.text:
`lib/` is not build output — it is the hand-written source, in the exact wire
format the DSH client module system loads. There is deliberately no `src/`, no
`scripts.build` and no `scripts.prepack`, so a clean checkout is already the
artifact and a GitHub install needs no `allowBuilds` approval.

`plugin_check` flags all three of those as warnings on the assumption that a
plugin is compiled; they are inapplicable here rather than unaddressed. The
package passes with **no errors**.

readme.section: For reviewers: why there is no build step
readme.text:
Run the checks yourself:

```sh
npm test              # all three suites below
npm run test:unit     # direction verdicts and the caret swap, against DOM stubs
npm run test:browser  # real layout in headless Chrome: GenUI steps, question
                      # cards, the user bubble, markdown blocks
